vignette: Thomas Vance was thirty-two when the Phoenix layover ended, but the memory that followed fractured his timeline. He had trusted Elias, a logistics officer who had shared a bottle of whiskey and insisted on driving him to a quiet hotel off-base. What happened inside that room was a violation that erased his assumptions about safety. He had let his guard down. He had expected boundaries to be respected. The betrayal cut deep, leaving Thomas certain that trust was always a prelude to ruin. That conviction now sits beside his other experiences, parallel and unyielding, without explanation or excuse. In the weeks that followed, Thomas’s days unfolded in overlapping layers of vigilance. He began waking with his pulse racing, the lingering pressure of a nightmare still pressed against his skin before his eyes even opened. Ordinary noises became jarring. The clatter of a coffee mug dropping in the kitchen, the sudden hiss of the refrigerator compressor—each made him jump, his shoulders tightening as if bracing for impact. Inside his own apartment, he found himself listening past the silence, straining to hear footsteps, the click of a deadbolt, or the rustle of someone slipping through the door. He felt on guard even behind his own closed windows, his posture rigid, his hands resting near the keys on the counter. When he moved through the squadron hangar during a routine maintenance walk, his attention snagged on anyone whose posture seemed off, whose eyes lingered too long, or whose movements felt deliberate in a way that felt wrong. What frightened him most was the way the hangar lights caught the faces of technicians, making him certain that a familiar smile could hide a threat. During a sudden weather diversion briefing, the captain changed the routing without warning. Thomas’s pen froze over the flight plan. He packed his bag immediately, citing fatigue, and walked out before the briefing concluded. His reactions since the event, he told himself, proved he was a lousy coper. The trust he once extended to his unit, to his community, to any notion of order, had curdled. He had lost his faith in people, in life, or in a higher power; the world no longer made sense. Over months, these patterns hardened into habits. He stopped answering calls after dark, cancelled dinner invitations before they were even made, and withdrew from the shared routines of squadron life. His supervisor noted the distance, the way Thomas’s once-precise flight checks grew hesitant, the way he sidestepped unpredictable tasking shifts. The consequences were quiet but real: his flight clearance was downgraded, his crew assignments suspended, and the isolation Thomas had adopted to navigate the triggers became a permanent fixture in his career. Now, sitting in the intake office, Thomas stares at his hands. He came because the weight has become impossible to carry alone, because he can no longer pretend the hypervigilance or the lingering dread are manageable. He is most afraid that he will never feel safe in his own skin again, that the betrayal will always color every room he walks into. Yet, beneath the fear, there is a quiet hope: a desire to sleep without waking startled, to look at the sky without bracing for an attack, to believe that trust might not always be a prelude to ruin.
